lesson.title: Scientific Notation: Taming Enormous and Tiny Numbers
lesson.summary: Scientific notation writes any number as a decimal between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, using integer exponents and the product rule to make extreme numbers easy to read, compare, and multiply.
lesson.body:
Some numbers in science and engineering are so large or so small that writing them out in full digits is impractical and error-prone. The distance across a galaxy or the mass of a single atom would take a page of zeros to write in ordinary decimal form. Scientific notation solves this by writing any number as a times 10 raised to an integer power, where a is a decimal number with exactly one nonzero digit before the decimal point, meaning 1 is less than or equal to the absolute value of a, which is less than 10. The power of ten does the work of tracking how many places the decimal point has shifted, which is exactly what integer exponents on the base 10 are built to do.

Converting a large number into scientific notation means moving the decimal point left until only one nonzero digit remains before it, then counting how many places you moved. Take 45,000,000. Moving the decimal point from the end of the number to just after the 4 takes 7 places, giving 4.5. So 45,000,000 = 4.5 times 10^7. You can check this by multiplying back out: 4.5 times 10^7 = 4.5 times 10,000,000 = 45,000,000, which matches.

Small numbers work the same way but the exponent turns negative, since you are moving the decimal point to the right instead of the left, which corresponds to dividing by powers of ten rather than multiplying. Take 0.00032. Moving the decimal point from its starting position to just after the 3 takes 4 places to the right, giving 3.2 times 10^-4. Checking this, 3.2 times 10^-4 = 3.2 divided by 10,000 = 0.00032, which matches.

Scientific notation becomes especially useful when multiplying extreme numbers, because the product rule for exponents lets you handle the powers of ten separately from the decimal parts. To multiply (3 times 10^4) by (2 times 10^3), multiply the decimal parts together and the powers of ten together: 3 times 2 = 6, and 10^4 times 10^3 = 10^(4+3) = 10^7 by the product rule. So the product is 6 times 10^7. As a check, 30,000 times 2,000 = 60,000,000, and 6 times 10^7 is also 60,000,000, so the two match.

Sometimes multiplying the decimal parts produces a number that is 10 or greater, which means the result is not yet in proper scientific notation and needs to be renormalized. For example, (5 times 10^3) times (4 times 10^2) gives 5 times 4 = 20 for the decimal part and 10^3 times 10^2 = 10^5 for the power of ten, so the raw product is 20 times 10^5. Since 20 is not between 1 and 10, rewrite it as 2.0 times 10^1, and combine that extra power of ten with the existing one: 2.0 times 10^(1+5) = 2.0 times 10^6. Checking against the standard form, 5,000 times 400 = 2,000,000, and 2.0 times 10^6 is also 2,000,000, confirming the answer.

Being comfortable with integer exponents on the base 10, including 10^0 = 1 and negative exponents such as 10^-1 = 0.1, is what makes every one of these conversions work smoothly, since each shift of the decimal point by one place corresponds to multiplying or dividing by exactly one factor of 10. Scientific notation is not a separate topic bolted onto exponents, it is a direct application of the exponent rules to a single, extremely useful base.
